sections.heading: Your first day, step by step
sections.body: A relaxed way to run day one, based on the confirmed mechanics:
items: Greet a walk-in customer
Small walk-ins are the safest first job — cheap, fast, and they teach the loop.
Open the device with your screwdriver
Get used to the disassembly step before taking anything apart at speed.
Write every state in your notebook
The notebook remembers for you — record dirty, broken and missing parts.
Clean what you can, replace what you must
Brush dirty parts; buy spares only for what is truly broken or missing.
Deliver and bank the profit
A clean delivery builds reputation and cash for your first upgrades.

sections.heading: What the notebook does for you
sections.body: The notebook is the game's memory (source: intoindiegames). Three things it changes:
items: No guessing
You never re-open a device wondering what was wrong — the state is written down.
Plans repairs
You decide what to clean vs replace before spending money.
Tracks every device
The full state of every device you have worked on stays available.

sections.heading: Repair habits that pay off
sections.body: Small habits with big returns over a playthrough:
items: Always record before cleaning — guessing costs money.
Prioritise walk-ins early, then grow into online orders.
Upgrade the screwdriver before anything else.
Feed spare parts to the shredder instead of hoarding them.
Keep a small parts stockpile for Frugal (10 days without buying).

sections.heading: More beginner questions
items: Should I take every online order?
No — take only what you can finish before the 3-day deadline. Reputation matters.
Is it okay to refuse a customer?
You can refuse payment (the Origami achievement), but otherwise keep the shop open to earn.
Do I need to repair everything in one day?
No — the game is chill; there is no fail state, only reputation for missed orders.
How do I know what to upgrade next?
Screwdriver first, brush second, then passive income (tip jar, shredder).

sections.heading: What to skip early
sections.body: The confirmed economy is clear about two money-pits (source: intoindiegames):
items: Painting devices — confirmed not profitable early; invest in repairs instead.
Reprogramming — same story: not a money-maker in the early game.
Stockpiling air cans — consumables; the brush covers most cleaning.
Over-buying parts — the notebook tells you exactly what you need.

sections.heading: First-day FAQ
items: Can I lose the game on day one?
No — there is no fail state; the worst outcome is reputation loss.
How many devices should I fix day one?
As many small ones as you enjoy — pace is yours.
Should I buy every tool immediately?
No — screwdriver first; buy others as jobs demand them.
Where does the money go first?
Screwdriver upgrade, then the tip jar for passive income.

sections.heading: Before you close the shop
sections.body: A short closing ritual that keeps progress smooth:
items: Fulfil any order with a deadline today.
Feed spare parts to the shredder for passive cash.
Save your progress and check tomorrow's order board.
Note which devices still need parts so tomorrow starts planned.

beginners-guide.intro_extra: The confirmed loop never changes: accept, disassemble, inspect, clean, replace, reassemble. Master it slowly and you will never need to rush — the game is designed to be relaxed, not stressful. Take it at your own pace: the shop never punishes a slow day, only missed promises. Above all, enjoy the shop: the game is built around the pace you set, and the guides here exist so nothing feels like a wall. When in doubt, choose the slower, cleaner repair — it builds the reputation that every later system feeds on.

sections.heading: Cleaning tools and when to use them
sections.body: A clean repair is a happy customer. Use tools in this order:
items: Brush first — it is reusable and covers most dirt.
Sonic bath for deep cleaning — timing matters.
Air can sparingly — it is a consumable; do not stockpile.
Check every part after cleaning so nothing dirty ships.

sections.heading: Repair details FAQ
items: What counts as a clean repair?
Every part cleaned, every broken/missing part replaced, and the device reassembled correctly.
Can I repair the same device twice?
Yes — devices return; the notebook keeps your history straight.
Do parts have states I can see?
Yes — clean, dirty, broken or missing; the notebook records them.
Is replacing always better than cleaning?
No — cleaning first saves money; replace only what is actually broken or missing.

sections.heading: The notebook at work
sections.body: A real repair flow with the notebook (source: intoindiegames):
items: Disassemble and lay parts out
Keep the order straight — the notebook records where things came from.
Write each part's state
Clean, dirty, broken or missing — one line per part.
Decide clean vs replace
Use the written states to avoid buying parts you only needed to clean.
Check off as you finish
Mark each part done so nothing ships half-fixed.

sections.heading: Signs of a good repair
items: Every dirty part cleaned, not just the visible ones.
Only truly broken/missing parts replaced — no wasted spend.
Assembly order matches disassembly notes.
Customer satisfied, reputation intact.

sections.heading: Quick repair checklist
sections.body: Run this on every device before delivery:
items: All dirty parts cleaned.
Broken or missing parts replaced.
Assembly order matches the notebook.
No deadline missed on the way out.

repair-guide.intro_extra: This page is the reference you will come back to: the loop, the notebook, the tools, and the mistakes that cost money. Keep this page open while you learn — every repair is the same loop, and the loop is easy once you see it whole.

The economy rewards patience: repair cleanly, resell smartly, and let passive income do the heavy lifting over time. Track your habits weekly — the shop that repairs cleanly, flips smartly and banks passive income is the shop that reaches Millionaire.
